"Speak Up or Shut Up? When Should Colleges Take Institutional Stances on Public Issues"
Date

Universities and colleges face increasing pressure to speak out on today's most contentious political, moral, and social issues. But when should an institution of higher learning take a stand—and when is silence the wiser choice? In The University's Voice, Steve Poskanzer P'15 offers a timely and practical guide for institutional leaders grappling with these high-stakes questions.

Economics Program in Cambridge (formerly Economics and European Studies) celebrated its 43rd anniversary in 2026. Since 1983, this program has engaged and challenged Carleton students to broaden and reimagine their world view through living and learning at one of the world’s great universities and exploring one of the world’s great capitals.

With decades of experience as a college president, Poskanzer examines the growing demands for universities to take official positions on matters ranging from climate change to global conflicts, to current debates over public policy. He argues that universities must be faithful to and focused upon their core mission—advancing knowledge and learning—while carefully navigating the fragile "social compact" between academia and broader society. At the heart of his argument is the "General Rule of Reticence," a principle that universities should be circumspect about adopting institutional positions unless doing so is essential to the pursuit of their mission, including safeguarding academic freedom. But reticence does not mean cowed silence. Poskanzer outlines clear, actionable criteria for when universities can and even must speak out: when they possess unique educational expertise to offer; when speech will ensure a robust intellectual environment for faculty and students; when their mission is at issue; or when their very existence is at risk.

Microbial proteins are the engines of major biogeochemical cycles, driving biochemical conversions and habitability in the surface ocean. Microbial metaproteomics enables a high-throughput glimpse into these microbial engines, including the interactions between microbial community members and their surrounding environments. The ProteOMZ research expedition surveyed the proteomes of the free-living microbial communities (0.2 to 3 µm) along a 5,000-km-long, 1-km-deep transect in the central Pacific Ocean. Eighty-five percent of total protein abundance was of bacterial origin, with Archaea contributing 1.6%. Over 2,000 functional KEGG Ontology (KO) groups were identified, yet only 25 KO groups contributed over half of the protein abundance, simultaneously indicating abundant key functions and a long tail of diverse functions. Community protein expression varied along horizontal and vertical scales, aligning with key environmental features of major oceanic regimes. Unsupervised clustering analyses revealed syntrophic dynamics between community members along the transect. High-throughput proteomic surveys can provide key insights into the integral microbial communities of the surface ocean and the key elemental cycles they mediate.

json.description:
Title: Reliable event rates for disease mapping

Abstract: When analyzing spatially referenced event data, the criteria for declaring rates as "reliable" is still a matter of dispute. What these varying criteria have in common, however, is that they are rarely satisfied for crude estimates in small area analysis settings, prompting the use of spatial models to improve reliability.  While reasonable, recent work has quantified the extent to which popular models from the spatial statistics literature can overwhelm the information contained in the data, leading to oversmoothing.  Here, we begin by providing a definition for a "reliable" estimate for event rates that can be used for crude and model-based estimates and allows for discrete and continuous statements of reliability.  After a brief introduction to Bayesian statistics, we then construct a spatial Bayesian framework that allows users to infuse prior information into their models to improve reliability while also guarding against oversmoothing. We apply our approach to county-level birth data from Pennsylvania, highlighting the effect of oversmoothing in spatial models and how our approach can allow users to better focus their attention to areas where sufficient data exists to drive inferential decisions.  We then conclude with a brief discussion of how this definition of reliability can be used in the design of small area studies.

json.description:
Bittersweet Homes: Placemaking in a Parish Haunted by History

This talk uses archival research and family memories to illuminate the lives and times of select figures who died and, critically, also lived in the long arc of King Cotton. Drawing on select moments in the history of the author's maternal grandmother's birthplace, Louisiana's Feliciana Parishes, it meditates on the deeply contingent experiences of 19th-Century "development" and "progress" and the ways those divergent experiences - and the memories to which they gave rise - haunt us all.

Rashauna Johnson is a historian of the 19th-century African diaspora, with an emphasis on slavery and emancipation in the US South and Atlantic World. She is especially interested in the limits and possibilities of archival histories of enslaved and freed people and the worlds in which they labored and lived. Johnson teaches courses on race, slavery, and nation; methodologies of slavery studies; and the 19th-century US.

Johnson is the author of Slavery’s Metropolis: Unfree Labor in New Orleans during the Age of Revolutions (Cambridge UP, 2016; paperback 2018), which was awarded the 2016 Williams Prize for the best book in Louisiana history and the 2018 H. L. Mitchell Award by the Southern Historical Association for the best book on the southern working class. Slavery's Metropolis was also named a finalist for the 2016 Berkshire Conference of Women's Historians Book Prize, honorable mention for the Urban History Association's Kenneth Jackson Award, and a finalist for the 2017 Frederick Douglass Book Prize. Her second book, Sweet Home Feliciana: Family, Slavery, and the Hauntings of History (Cambridge University Press, 2026), uses her grandmother’s birthplace in rural Louisiana as a prism to illuminate foundational, if fraught, aspects of US history including colonialism, slavery, war, citizenship and unfinished freedom. That project has been supported by the Hutchins Center for African & African American Research at Harvard University, the Mellon Scholars Post-Doctoral Fellowship in African American History at the Library Company of Philadelphia, and The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History. She is a co-editor of the Cambridge History of the African Diaspora, Volume Two: Slave Trades, Dispersals, and Processes of Commodification (forthcoming 2027).

json.description:
Navigating the complexities of eldercare—from managing medical appointments and legal paperwork to the emotional weight of changing family roles—is a journey few of us are prepared for. Whether you are currently providing daily care for an aging parent, supporting an adult friend through a health crisis, or simply beginning to plan for the future, you don't have to manage it in isolation. 
We hope to provide a dedicated space where we can find both practical resources and authentic peer support. By coming together, we can share vetted local resources, navigate insurance and healthcare hurdles, and offer a listening ear to those balancing professional excellence with personal sacrifice.


 	Resource Sharing: Access to curated lists of local home-health services, elder law specialists, and respite care.
 	Regular Meet-ups: Informal gatherings to discuss challenges and successes.
 	Expert Guest Speakers: Occasional sessions with professionals in gerontology, financial planning, and mental health.

Taking care of those who once took care of us is a profound responsibility, but it can also be an exhausting one. We invite you to join us for our inaugural meeting to help shape this group into a community that truly serves your needs. Together, we can ensure that as we care for others, we are also caring for ourselves.

Jack El-Hai is a journalist who writes nonfiction books, articles, and essays. He covers medicine, history, science, and crime.

Among his published books are The New York Times bestselling The Nazi and the Psychiatrist (adapted in 2025 into the movie Nuremberg), The Lobotomist, The Lost Brothers, and Face in the Mirror. His new book The Case of the Autographed Corpse: A Medicine Man and a Mystery Writer in Pursuit of Justice will be published by Pegasus Books in October 2026. He has contributed essays and articles to Smithsonian, The Atlantic, GQ, Wired, Scientific American, and many other publications. Since 2018, he has published “Damn History,” a free monthly newsletter for readers and writers of popular history.

Jack grew up in Los Angeles and is a past president of the American Society of Journalists and Authors. He is a two-time winner of the June Roth Award for medical journalism and has won two Minnesota Book Awards. He currently sits on the board of The Loft Literary Center in Minneapolis. His website is https://el-hai.com.

His presentation is titled Writing to Change Hearts and Minds.

Sound Bath Meditation in partnership with The Office of Health Promotion led by Marc Anderson.

An immersive experience in which the listener is “bathed” in waves of soft tones, shifting textures and gentle rhythms. Combining the sounds of crystal singing bowls, gongs, hand drums and subtle drones Marc creates a rich and deeply therapeutic experience. His extensive background as a musician and meditation teacher, supported by years of studying trance related music/healing traditions, allows him to create unique, powerful, well-crafted sessions that restore, relax and transform.

Marc Anderson is a Twin Cities based musician, composer, Zen priest and poet. He has studied, performed and recorded music all over the world with hundreds of great artists including; Angelique Kidjo, Robert Fripp, Steve Tibbetts, Don Cherry, Max Roach and Taj Mahal. He founded and directs the M2 Foundation which advocates for a more mindful and compassionate world. And, he is on staff in the Center for Religious and Spiritual Life at Macalester College.

json.description:
For generations, Indigenous science has been dismissed as folklore rather than recognized as rigorous, land-based knowledge accumulated through direct relationship with ecosystems. Dr. Jessica Hernandez (Maya Ch'orti' & Binnizá) draws on her work as founder of Earth Daughters and author of Fresh Banana Leaves and Growing Papaya Trees to reframe the climate conversation: colonialism didn't just displace Indigenous peoples from their lands, it displaced their knowledge systems from the institutions now scrambling to solve the crisis those systems could have prevented. This keynote traces the throughline from ecological healing to climate displacement, and makes the case that climate justice is inseparable from Indigenous sovereignty; over land, over research, and over the frameworks we use to define what counts as science.

json.description:
In 1972, between 100,000 and 300,000 Burundians, overwhelmingly Hutu, were killed in a campaign that targeted the educated and hollowed out communities across the country. It remains one of the least acknowledged genocides of the twentieth century, absent from international memory and long unspeakable within Burundi itself.

Jeanine Ntihirageza was eleven when her father and brother were killed. She did not learn until two years later that she was Hutu, and that this was why they died. In this lecture, she traces her journey from imposed silence to public mourning, and from the mind's decision to forgive to forgiveness of the heart. She also traces the path that led her from linguistics to genocide scholarship.

Drawing on that experience and on years of gathering survivor testimony in Burundi and the diaspora, she argues that silence is not merely the aftermath of genocide but one of its instruments. She shows how memory survives anyway: in the Kirundi language, in families, in diaspora communities, and in Ubuntu ethics of shared humanity. The lecture asks what human rights frameworks miss when they treat African survivors as victims to be documented rather than as knowers. It closes by asking what responsible remembering demands of audiences far from the events.

Dr. Ntihirageza's visit to campus is organized by the Africana Studies program via the generous support of the Division of Inclusion, Equity and Community and Ethical Inquiry at Carleton (EthIC).

---------------

Jeanine Ntihirageza is Professor of Linguistics and TESOL at Northeastern Illinois University and founder of its Center for Genocide and Human Rights Research in Africa and the Diaspora (GHRAD). She is a survivor of the 1972 genocide against Hutu in Burundi, in which she lost her father, her brother, and other relatives when she was eleven years old. She began her career as a teacher in Burundi and earned a PhD in Linguistics from the University of Chicago, specializing in Bantu languages. Her path from linguist to genocide scholar led to work that decolonizes the field by centering African epistemologies, Ubuntu philosophy, and survivor testimony. She is a Senior Research Associate at the University of Johannesburg's African Centre for Epistemology and Philosophy of Science, a Commissioner on the Illinois Holocaust and Genocide Commission, and an editorial board member of Cambridge Elements in Genocide Studies.

Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice unexpected objects or events when a person is focusing their attention on something else. It is a side effect of our remarkable and essential ability to focus attention and ignore distractions, but it can have real consequences. In this presentation, Dr. Dan Simons will describe recent (and older) research on inattentional blindness both in and out of the lab. This talk is part of the Edwin L. Weisl Jr. Lecture Series sponsored by the Robert Lehman Foundation

Architectural historian and activist, Patricia Morton will give a talk that focuses on writings and buildings by Charles W. Moore, a prominent Postmodern architect, who asserted that “you have to pay for the public life” in a famous 1965 essay. Looking at several of Moore’s projects from the 1960s and 1970s, the talk will investigate what Moore meant by “paying” for the public realm, his advocacy for Disneyland as a public space, and the ways he understood “the public” in various contexts, including a public housing project and student housing at a public university



Patricia A. Morton is Associate Professor in the Media and Cultural Studies Department at the University of California, Riverside.

She is author of Hybrid Modernities: Architecture and Representation at the 1931 International Colonial Exposition in Paris (MIT Press). Her current project, Paying for the Public Life, focuses on work by architect Charles W. Moore and changes to the public realm in the 1960s.

Navigating the complexities of eldercare—from managing medical appointments and legal paperwork to the emotional weight of changing family roles—is a journey few of us are prepared for. Whether you are currently providing daily care for an aging parent, supporting an adult friend through a health crisis, or simply beginning to plan for the future, you don't have to manage it in isolation. 
We hope to provide a dedicated space where we can find both practical resources and authentic peer support. By coming together, we can share vetted local resources, navigate insurance and healthcare hurdles, and offer a listening ear to those balancing professional excellence with personal sacrifice.


 	Resource Sharing: Access to curated lists of local home-health services, elder law specialists, and respite care.
 	Regular Meet-ups: Informal gatherings to discuss challenges and successes.
 	Expert Guest Speakers: Occasional sessions with professionals in gerontology, financial planning, and mental health.

Taking care of those who once took care of us is a profound responsibility, but it can also be an exhausting one. We invite you to join us for our inaugural meeting to help shape this group into a community that truly serves your needs. Together, we can ensure that as we care for others, we are also caring for ourselves.

json.description:
As two countries with sizable Black populations but very different histories, Colombia and Brazil offer a fascinating contrast for understanding blackness in Latin America.  Historically, Colombia largely denied its black population’s importance to its national identity, yet Afro-Colombian culture has thrived and influenced the larger culture in multiple ways.  In contrast, Brazil declared itself a multiracial nation as early as the 1930s–but this did not lead to the racial democracy that was officially declared by the government.   Both countries have gone through significant political and social changes in the past three decades that have impacted and shaped Afrodescendant communities and identities.  In this program, we explore contemporary Afro-Brazilian and Afro-Colombian identities, cultures, and communities with a particular focus on regional differences and social change and movements. As a two-country program that takes place in four cities, this program offers multiple opportunities for intellectually rich comparisons and reflections on transnational blackness, national and regional identities, and culture and power in Latin America.

A Native American activist, Harvard-educated economist and author, Winona LaDuke has devoted her life to advocating for indigenous people’s rights; environmental justice; women's and children's rights; rural development, economic, food, and energy sovereignty.

The Convocation presentation is called Creating a Multicultural Democracy - Religion, Culture, and Identity in America! 

In 1985, LaDuke co-founded and co-chaired the Indigenous Women’s Network (IWN), a coalition dedicated to empowering women to take active roles in tribal politics and culture. In 1989, she founded the White Earth Land Recovery Project (WELRP), a reservation-based land acquisition, environmental advocacy, and cultural organization and one of the largest reservation-based nonprofits in the country. She is a former board member of Greenpeace USA. In 1993, she collaborated with the Indigo Girls to co-found Honor the Earth, an advocacy group working on behalf of Native environmental groups.

In 1994, LaDuke was nominated by Time Magazine as one of America’s 50 most promising leaders under the age of 40. She was awarded The Thomas Merton Award in 1996, The Biha Community Service Award in n 1997, The Ann Bancroft Award for Women’s Leadership Fellowship, and The Reebok Human Rights Award (which she used to begin the White Earth Land Recovery Project). LaDuke was a two-time Green Party running mate for Ralph Nader in 1996 and 2000, and she is an international thought leader and lecturer in climate justice, renewable energy and environmental justice, plus an advocate for protecting Indigenous plants and heritage foods from patenting and genetic engineering.

In 1998, Ms. Magazine named her one of their Women of the Year. In 2021, LaDuke was named to the first Forbes list of “50 Over 50 Women of Impact” in partnership with Mika Brzezinski’s “Know Your Value,” a program dedicated to shining a light on women over the age of 50 who have achieved significant success later in life, often overcoming formidable odds or barriers. She was a leader at the 2016 Dakota Access Pipeline protests that sought to protect water access and sacred Indigenous lands in North Dakota, and her work inspired the 2017 documentary First Daughter and the Black Snake. In 2017, LaDuke also won the University of California’s Alice and Clifford Spendlove Prize in Social Justice, Diplomacy and Tolerance.

LaDuke has published six acclaimed nonfiction titles, including: The Militarization of Indian Country; Recovering the Sacred: The Power of Naming and Claiming; All Our Relations: Native Struggles for Land and Life; The Winona LaDuke Chronicles: Stories from the Front Lines in the Battle for Environmental Justice; The Winona LaDuke Reader: A Collection of Essential Writings; and most recently, To Be a Water Protector: Rise of the Wiindigoo Slayers—a book that deals with her activism battling Line 3, an Enbridge tar sands oil pipeline in northern Minnesota. She is also the author of one novel, Last Standing Woman.

Today, Winona LaDuke lives and works on the White Earth reservation in northern Minnesota, and she is active with multiple organizations, including the Anishinaabe Agriculture Institute, Akiing. Her latest effort is Winona’s Hemp and Heritage, a farm and nonprofit agency whose mission is to create an Indigenous women-led economy that is kind to the Earth.

This convocation is also presented as a virtual webinar. Please register in advance if you would like to attend via Zoom. After registering, you will receive a confirmation email containing information about joining the webinar.

json.description:
"When we walk into a 'natural'  area, it can feel like we're entering an eternal space. This can deceive. The area that is now Carleton College's Arb has changed and changed again over its human history, and how people have regarded the land has changed, too. We'll look at the Arboretum as Dakota land; as small farms; in its first era as Carleton's Arboretum and Farm; in its role as a rougher, unchaperoned space in the turbulent 1960s; and in its newest transformation over the last 50 years into a treasured, organized part of the Carleton project."

Please join us for the second presentation of the Arboretum Centennial Speaker Series, The Six Lives of the Cowling Arboretum with Ingrid Case '90 and Nat Case ('88), co-authors of the recently published book, Into the Arb : a history of the Cowling Arboretum at Carleton College.
